newsitem.title: FRANCE: ERAMET URGES TALKS ON N CALEDONIA SMELTER.
newsitem.headline: ERAMET URGES TALKS ON N CALEDONIA SMELTER.

text.p: The chairman of French nickel producer Eramet said on Friday that all interested parties must work together to find a solution for a controversial plan to build a new nickel smelter in northern New Caledonia.

In a television interview Yves Rambaud reaffirmed Eramet supported plans by another group to build the plant as long as it did not threaten Eramet's development in the region, particularly of its Doniambo smelter near Noumea.
"We support the construction of a plant in the north... but it is obvious that it cannot be to the disadvantage of the Doniambo plant," Rambaud told RFO television.
"All industrial players involved must sit down and try to find the means, with or without us, to build that plant, which must be a great ambition for the territory," he added.
Eramet and the French government have been caught in a war of nerves over the distribution of mining reserves in New Caledonia.
The government, which owns 55 percent of Eramet, has launched a procedure to take away the firm's mining licence for the Koniambo mine in South Pacific island.
The government wants to hand the concession to local Kanak interests, stating Eramet has not operated the mine for 10 years. The Kanaks seek greater autonomy from France for New Caledonia.
Koniambo mining reserves would be used to supply ore to a nickel plant that Canadian group Falconbridge and local Kanak Societe Miniere de Sud Pacifique (SMSP) want to build.
The project is part of a deal to appease Kanaks ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence for the French territory.
The government came up with the plan to withdraw the licence after talks failed between Eramet's Societe le Nickel (SLN) and SMSP over an asset swap.
Eramet has said it would use all legal means available to prevent the licence withdrawal, arguing it was unjustified and would hurt its financial outlook.
Rambaud told RFO the loss of the licence would hurt the future of the Doniambo plant, possibly putting over 2,000 jobs at risk.
"If we lack the ore to supply the plant, we will have to slow down production at the plant," he said.
Eramet argues that the Koniambo mine is crucial to its plans to increase nickel production in New Caledonia to between 60,000 and 65,000 tonnes from the year 2000 from a current 54,000 tonnes.
Because the licence was given freely, Eramet would get no compensation for its loss but the government has said it plans to start separate talks over compensation.

Some investment funds like Fidelity have warned the government of possible consequences of, for example the sale of France Telecom shares if France did not respect the interest of Eramet's minority shareholders.
On April 3 Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said minority shareholders would be compensated for the licence loss.
Rambaud welcomed the news but said "compensation will not (help) supply the Domiambo smelter. An electric oven cannot be fed with a cheque."
Rambaud also said the method used by the government until now was hurting the image of both Eramet and New Caledonia.

"The method followed (until now) has proven it was not the right one. It is important to say and to confirm that we favour this project and that we are ready to participate in any serious study on the project," he said.

Rambaud said that future talks must clarify several issues, including how much ore would be needed to supply the plant in the north, how much ore SMSP would be able to supply from its reserves and what other producers, including Eramet, may have to contribute to make up for the ore shortfall.

Rambaud said that 120,000 tonnes of nickel are currently extracted in New Caledonia of which 50,000 tonnes are processed locally by Eramet. The remaining 70,000 tonnes is exported by other mining companies, including the SMSP, which recently signed a large export contract to supply a Japanese company.
